title: H-Index
prompt: Given an array of integers `citations` where `citations[i]` is the number of citations a researcher received for their `i`th paper, return the researcher's h-index. The h-index is defined as the maximum value `h` such that the researcher has published at least `h` papers that have each been cited at least `h` times (and the remaining papers have no more than `h` citations each, which is automatically satisfied by the maximum such h).

examples.explanation: The researcher has 3 papers with at least 3 citations each (6, 5, 3), and the other two have no more than 3.
With zero citations on every paper, not even a single paper has at least 1 citation, so the h-index is 0.

hints: Trying every possible h value and counting qualifying papers for each is O(n^2). Sorting the citations opens a faster path.
If you sort citations in descending order, the h-index is the last position (1-indexed) where the citation count is still >= that position's rank.

Walk the sorted-descending array with an index i (1-indexed rank); the h-index is the largest i such that citations[i-1] >= i, since beyond that point papers stop having enough citations to support a higher h.

solution.approach: Sort the citations in descending order. Walking through the sorted array, the 1-indexed position i represents 'at least i papers have this many citations or more' (since everything before it in descending order is >= it). The h-index is the largest i for which citations[i-1] is still >= i; once citations[i-1] drops below i, no larger h can be supported since sorting guarantees all later papers have fewer citations. A single linear scan over the sorted array finds this crossover point directly.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra space, excluding sort space
